title: Punnett squares
examples: How do I set up the square if I know the parents' genotypes?
If I use capital letters for dominant traits, what do I use for recessive ones?
Can I use this for more than two genes at once?

explain.say: Today we are learning about predicting traits in offspring.
First we look at monohybrid crosses to see one trait.
A monohybrid cross uses one specific gene pair from each parent.
Next we understand the resulting ratios of the traits.
Probability helps us find the chance of a specific outcome.
For a real-life example consider dog coat color inheritance.

faq.a: It means an organism has two different alleles for a particular gene. For example, one capital letter and one small letter.
asks: What is the meaning of Aa?

faq.q: How do I calculate the probability if the parents are different?
faq.a: You calculate the probability for each trait separately and then multiply them together. For instance, the chance of A from parent one times the chance of B from parent two.
asks: What if the parents are AA and aa?

faq.q: Are the ratios the same for genotypes and phenotypes?
faq.a: No, they are not always the same. The genotypic ratio describes the actual alleles present, while the phenotypic ratio describes the observable traits.
asks: Which ratio is more important to remember?

faq.q: Can I use Punnett squares for more than one trait?
faq.a: You can use them, but the squares become very large very quickly. It is often easier to use separate probability calculations for each trait.
asks: How big does the square get?
Is there a simpler way for two traits?

faq.q: What do the capital and small letters represent?
faq.a: The capital letter represents the dominant allele, which shows its trait. The small letter represents the recessive allele, which is only seen if two copies are present.

facts: Alleles are different versions of the same gene.
Dominant alleles mask the presence of recessive alleles.
A monohybrid cross tracks the inheritance of one specific trait.
The probability of an event is the ratio of favorable outcomes to total outcomes.

quiz.say: If a parent is Bb and another parent is Bb, what is the probability of the offspring being BB?
quiz.why: The only way to get BB is if both parents contribute the B allele, which happens one time out of four combinations.

wrong.0: This is common because students only consider the chance of getting a dominant trait.
wrong.1: This mistake happens when students incorrectly multiply the probabilities for each allele.
wrong.2: This suggests the student is calculating the probability for two separate, unrelated events.

quiz.say: In a cross between a dominant-dominant parent (AA) and a recessive-recessive parent (aa), what is the resulting phenotypic ratio?
quiz.why: All offspring must receive one A from the first parent and one a from the second parent, resulting only in the dominant phenotype.

wrong.0: This suggests the student is incorrectly dividing the possible outcomes into groups.
wrong.2: This ratio is typically seen in a cross between two heterozygous parents.
wrong.3: This ratio is the standard outcome for any monohybrid cross involving heterozygotes.

quiz.say: If the probability of an offspring having the genotype Aa is 2/4, what is the probability of it being homozygous recessive (aa)?
quiz.why: The total probability must equal one. If Aa is two quarters, then aa must be the remaining one quarter.

wrong.0: This mistake occurs when students only look at the two extreme possibilities, ignoring the middle one.
wrong.1: This suggests the student is treating the probabilities as sequential events rather than parts of a whole.
wrong.3: Students sometimes assume that the probability of one outcome equals the probability of another.
